video_title: The AI Enshittification Bubble | Cory Doctorow
gist: Cory Doctorow argues that AI is a fundamentally different bubble from web 1.0/2.0 because its unit economics are inverted — every incremental user and every model generation loses more money — so the AI incumbents are squeezing customers out of desperation rather than post-saturation greed. He ties this to his enshittification framework (removal of competition, IP-law-enabled anti-modification, and the collapse of tech-worker bargaining power) and to the 'reverse centaur' labor thesis, in which the AI investment case only pencils if buyers use it to cut headcount and turn survivors into machine-paced code auditors who absorb the blame.

themes.theme: Why the constraints on firms disappeared

insights.claim: Doctorow's core causal claim is that services got worse not because firms changed but because four external disciplines — competition, regulation, interoperability/self-help, and worker refusal — were systematically dismantled over 25 years, making abuse the highest-return strategy.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Frames degradation of product quality as a policy-driven, reversible regime rather than a permanent feature — policy shifts on antitrust or anti-circumvention law are the catalyst to watch for a repricing of platform moats.
insights.quote: And my thesis is that for the last 25 years, we've been systematically dismantling the sources of discipline on firms such that the worst people at the worst companies who have the worst ideas make the most money.

insights.claim: Section 1201 of the 1998 Digital Millennium Copyright Act — a felony carrying a 5-year sentence and $500,000 fine for modifying technology designed not to be modified — is the legal mechanism that lets firms wrap products in IP so competitors cannot build counter-tools, which is why browsers have ad blockers and apps do not.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Anti-circumvention law is the durable moat behind app-based and subscription-locked business models; any legislative or judicial narrowing of it would directly threaten aftermarket-lock-in revenue streams.
insights.quote: Almost everyone who has a web browser has an ad blocker. No one who uses an app has an ad blocker because reverse engineering an app is a felony under a law called the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.

insights.claim: The inkjet aftermarket is Doctorow's canonical example of IP-enabled rent extraction: a cartel of four firms controls the market and sells ink at roughly $10,000 a gallon because it is illegal to sell a tool that disables the printer's generic-ink check.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Consumables/subscription-lock margins in hardware depend on legal protection, not engineering — a regulatory or right-to-repair shock compresses them fast.
insights.quote: there's a cartel of four firms that control the inkjet market because again, we stopped enforcing antitrust laws

insights.claim: Tech workers' bargaining power came from scarcity plus productivity — a new Silicon Valley engineer adds roughly $1 million to the bottom line — and because they never converted that scarcity into unionized solidarity, roughly half a million layoffs over three years erased their ability to refuse orders to degrade products.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Explains why product quality and internal ethical friction collapsed post-layoffs; implies margin expansion at platforms now faces no internal brake, and perks/comp are structurally deflating.
insights.quote: There weren't 10 bosses at the factory gates who wanted to give them a job. There were 10 workers at the factory gates who wanted to take their job.

themes.theme: The platform decay cycle, told through Facebook

insights.claim: Doctorow's three-stage-plus-coda platform cycle runs: be good to users while locking them in via the collective action problem, then degrade users to please business customers, then extract from business customers too until only a 'homeopathic residue' of value remains.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: A reusable diagnostic for staging any platform investment — the terminal stage is a brittle equilibrium where a single shock triggers user flight, so late-stage platforms deserve a lower multiple, not a higher one.

insights.claim: Monopsony — power over locked-in suppliers — is more effective and more overlooked than monopoly, because controlling a business that derives 20% of its revenue from you is easier than controlling a customer who has 20% of supply available elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Screen platform dependency risk on the supplier side — publishers, app developers and sellers with high single-platform revenue concentration are the most exposed to margin extraction.
insights.quote: It's much easier to control a business with 20% of the market than it is to control a customer with 20% of the supply.

insights.claim: Procter & Gamble zeroed out a $200 million-a-year surveillance advertising budget in 2017 and saw a 0% drop in sales, which Doctorow reads as evidence that to a first approximation those ads were absorbed by fraud.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: A concrete precedent for advertiser-side revolt: if large brand budgets re-test attribution, platform ad revenue has more downside than consensus assumes.
insights.quote: 2017, Proctor and Gamble zeroed out their $200 million a year surveillance advertising spend.

insights.claim: Platform equity is priced for perpetual growth, so even a modest growth miss triggers violent repricing — Doctorow cites Q1 2022, when Zuckerberg's slightly-below-expectation US growth produced a one-day $240 billion sell-off he calls the largest decapitalization in market history.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Saturation, not competition, is the real tail risk in mega-cap platform positions; growth-rate disclosure dates are the asymmetric event risk.
insights.quote: first quarter 2022 when Zuckerberg announced slightly lower than anticipated US growth and there was a one-day $240 billion sell-off. It was the largest decation of any firm in the history of markets.

insights.claim: The web's unit economics improved with every additional user, session and generation, whereas AI inverts all three: each new user costs the provider money, heavier usage loses more money, and each successive model generation loses more than the last.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: If true, AI revenue growth is a cost accelerant rather than an operating-leverage story — usage metrics should be read as burn indicators, not as evidence of a path to profit.
insights.quote: Every new user that an AI company acquires costs them money. the more money the more that user uses AI, the more money they lose. Basically, AI companies are selling $100 bills for a dollar a piece.

insights.claim: The standard 'bubbles are useful because a bankruptcy leaves cheap capex behind' defense fails for AI because frontier and foundation models carry extremely high operating expenditure, unlike dark fiber where wiping out capex leaves a viable low-opex business.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Undercuts the popular 'we'll get cheap AI infrastructure after the crash' trade — the salvage value of a busted AI buildout may be far lower than the telecom analogy implies.

insights.claim: Low switching costs between models destroy the 'build one winning model and coast' thesis — Doctorow points to users abandoning ChatGPT for Claude, which forces OpenAI to spend hundreds of billions on the next model or die, and then forces Anthropic to respond in turn.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Implies no terminal-value moat at the model layer and a permanent capex treadmill — model labs may be structurally uninvestable relative to layers with real lock-in.
insights.quote: when someone comes out with a better model like Claude is currently better than chat GPT, the switching costs are really low. Everyone just switches, right? Everyone gave up on chat GPT and went to to claude

insights.claim: Doctorow distinguishes two kinds of squeeze: incumbent platforms like Google, Facebook, Apple, Microsoft and Oracle degrade products to extract extra profit from an already-good business, while AI companies would be squeezing because they are doomed and drowning.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: A test for reading price hikes and feature paywalls: at cash-generative incumbents they signal margin harvest; at AI pure-plays they may signal a solvency scramble.
insights.quote: there's like a big difference between a company that squeezes you in order to extract more revenue and a company that squeezes you because they're doomed

insights.claim: Doctorow treats non-GAAP profitability claims as a red flag rather than a nuance, singling out SoftBank — backer of WeWork, Uber and a large OpenAI investment — as the specialist in declaring loss-making businesses profitable under self-invented accounting standards.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: A simple screen for AI-adjacent holdings: demand GAAP figures, and treat adjusted-profitability disclosures from the SoftBank orbit as evidence of the opposite.
insights.quote: anytime someone tells you we're profitable but not according to GAP, you should reach for your wallet.

insights.claim: Doctorow endorses reporter Ed Zitron's analysis of leaked AI financials showing suspiciously small inference spend alongside marketing spend rivaling or exceeding Coca-Cola's, and argues the discrepancy is explained by subsidized inference being booked as marketing.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: If free-tier compute is classified as customer acquisition rather than cost of revenue, headline gross margins at AI labs are overstated — a specific line item to interrogate in any disclosure.
insights.quote: what they've done is they've they've uh hidden inference in their balance sheet as marketing

insights.claim: Doctorow describes tech reporting as 'Texas marksman' behavior — firing a shotgun at a barn then drawing the target around the pellets — arguing platforms select whichever monthly metric flatters them and then declare it the headline number.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Treat newly introduced or redefined KPIs at platforms and AI firms as a signal of deterioration in the metric they replaced.
insights.quote: these guys get to just um be Texas marksmen, so they they they fire a shotgun into the side of a barn and then draw a target around the place where the pellets went in

insights.claim: AI benchmark progress is self-refuting in Doctorow's reading: improving on an existing benchmark shows only tuning skill, while shifting to new benchmarks concedes that the old improvement curve stopped — and the investor case requires continuous rapid improvement to justify over a trillion dollars spent in the last year.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Benchmark headlines are the load-bearing input to AI capex justification; treating them as marketing rather than measurement changes the terminal-value math.
insights.quote: That doesn't tell you that the bots are getting smarter. That tells me that you're getting better at tuning bots to whatever.

themes.theme: Growth narratives as a capital-raising machine

insights.claim: Doctorow's mechanism for narrative escalation is material rather than ideological: a growth multiple lets a firm pay for talent and acquisitions in liquid stock, so when growth stalls the stock currency degrades, key staff demand cash, and acquisitions and hiring become exponentially harder — a self-accelerating collapse.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Explains why saturating platforms fight so hard for a new story — and why stock-funded acquirers unwind faster than balance sheets alone suggest once the multiple compresses.
insights.quote: if you can buy another company by using stock, then all you have to do is type some zeros into a spreadsheet and you own another company.

insights.claim: Doctorow argues firms shifted from 'we'll eat a rival's lunch' narratives to invented-market narratives — metaverse, NFTs, blockchain, web3 — precisely because a nonexistent market's TAM cannot be rebutted with facts, whereas Facebook can credibly deny that a competitor is becoming Facebook.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Unfalsifiable TAM estimates from research houses are a tell for narrative-stage capital cycles — treat them as a sell signal, not a sizing input.
insights.quote: who is anyone to argue with you about the size of that market opportunity? You literally just made it up.

insights.claim: The scale gap between the metaverse and AI bets is roughly an order of magnitude: Doctorow cites Facebook's ~$61 billion metaverse loss against $150 billion spent over the last three years, another $150 billion lost this year on AI, and guidance for more than $150 billion of losses next year.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Sizes the downside if the AI narrative breaks — a metaverse-style write-off at this scale is a multi-hundred-billion-dollar event, not a one-quarter charge.
insights.quote: They spent $150 billion of the last three years. They lost another $150 billion this year on AI. And they're saying that they're going to lose more next year, more than 150 billion.

insights.claim: The host argues this cycle is more dangerous than the crypto bubble because crypto's narrative required almost no capital expenditure, whereas the AI narrative is directly tied to physical capex — and notes that companies like SpaceX, whose revenue he believes is largely advertising-driven, are rebranding themselves into the AI story.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Capex-anchored narratives leave stranded physical assets and creditor claims when they break, making the unwind slower and more systemically visible than crypto's.
insights.quote: the last big bubble with the crypto bubble wasn't a high capex bubble. Like you didn't need to expend a ton of capital in order to sell a narrative. In this case, the narrative is tied to the capital expenditures.

themes.theme: Reverse centaurs: the labor case underneath AI valuations

insights.claim: Doctorow's automation-adoption rule is that capital adopts automation to raise throughput while labor adopts it to raise quality, and where a monopoly or duopoly exists the firm can cut quality and raise throughput simultaneously and pocket the difference.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Predicts where AI deployment shows up as measurable service degradation rather than customer benefit — concentrated industries with captive customers.
insights.quote: when capital drives uh automation adoption, it tends to do so in service to increase throughput

insights.claim: A centaur is a human assisted by a machine — the human supplies judgment — while a reverse centaur is a human conscripted to serve the machine, and because the human is the slowest component the machine paces them at the absolute limit of their endurance.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: A concrete lens for evaluating AI deployment claims: ask who sets the pace and who holds discretion, which determines whether productivity gains are real or extracted from worker attrition.
insights.quote: It's the horse's head on the human body. It's the machine driving the person. It's when a person is conscripted to serve the machine.

insights.claim: Amazon's most-automated warehouses also have the highest injury rates, which Doctorow attributes to capex logic rather than accident: seven- and eight-figure machines are run at maximum speed, forcing the humans in the loop to match that speed until they slip.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Injury and turnover data are an observable proxy for reverse-centaur deployment and a source of regulatory and litigation risk for automation-heavy operators.
insights.quote: Amazon has built the most automated warehouses the world has ever seen. And they are also the warehouses with the highest rate of injury.

insights.claim: Doctorow explicitly rejects the 'AI makes you stupid or addictive' critiques as overblown while fully endorsing the labor critique — that AI is bought to fire workers and to make survivors do two jobs and absorb the blame when things break.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Positions the AI investment case as fundamentally a labor-cost-arbitrage bet, so enterprise headcount and severance data are the real read-through for AI ROI.
insights.quote: your boss bought AI because he wants to either fire you or fire the person who works next to you and make you do the job of two people and then blame you if anything goes wrong. I think those people are 100% right.

insights.claim: The contradictory testimony of programmers — some report becoming far better engineers with AI, others report unprecedented tech debt — is resolved by who controls the deployment, with the negative group having lost nine of ten colleagues and been made the 'accountability sink' reviewing AI code at impossible speed.
insights.speaker: Cory Doctorow
insights.so_what: Explains why AI productivity studies conflict, and flags accumulating unreviewed tech debt in safety-critical sectors as a deferred liability that does not show up in current earnings.
insights.quote: I have never made so much tech debt in my life. I work in avionics. Never get on a plane again. I think the whole civilian aviation industry is now doomed. We are shoveling tech debt into airplanes at a rate never seen.
